hook: A 1922 commercial building on the site of an 1847 O'Farrell land grant, later the California Historical Society's headquarters for 31 years.

parcel.note: Business addresses are usually deferred on this site; this page exists because the prompting source locates a resolvable 1847 land grant here, at the site of a named present-day building. The assessor's property_location and DBI's permit records both name this parcel 666 Mission Street. EAS separately carries 678 Mission Street with no parcel_number of its own, but 678 is the address the California Historical Society used for the same building during its 1993–2024 tenancy, on the same Mission Street frontage as 666.

assessment.exemption: Welfare exemption (nonprofit use), while the California Historical Society held the parcel

permits.description: Cellular communication installed for the fire alarm system, a like-for-like replacement under a 2008 state fire marshal bulletin.
Fire sprinkler system installed in the basement.
New handicap bathrooms; rotted stair and roll-up gate replaced.

historical_record.description: The California Historical Society announced its permanent closure and the transfer of its collection to Stanford University, which holds it as the California History Collection.
The Society sold the building, by then vacated, for about $6.7 million to a limited liability company affiliated with the San Francisco Baking Institute.

The California Historical Society sold the parcel's transferable development rights, which limits any future redevelopment to repurposing the existing two-story building rather than building to the site's zoned height.

historical_record.summary: Purchased by the California Historical Society
historical_record.description: The California Historical Society purchased the building for $2 million and made it its headquarters, converting the basement under the Mission Street sidewalk into climate-controlled collection storage and adding seismic upgrades, a public research library, exhibition galleries and a bookstore.
Hundley Hardware Company's occupancy of the building ended.
The San Francisco Builders Exchange occupied the building.
Architect Andrew H. Knoll designed the two-story Renaissance Revival building on the site, built for the Phoenix Desk and Chair Company.
Acting Alcalde Hyde granted Jasper O'Farrell's petition for a 100-vara lot on the north side of Mission Street, between 100-vara grants to Col. John C. Fremont and Alcalde Washington Bartlett.
Jasper O'Farrell petitioned Acting Alcalde Hyde for the grant of the 100-vara lot.
